title: Every WW2 Rifle RANKED — WORST to BEST
fullText: By 1945, most soldiers on Earth were still fighting with a rifle design older than their grandfathers. A bolt you had to yank by hand between every single shot. But buried in that same war was a weapon so far ahead of everyone else that soldiers are still carrying its grandchildren into battle today. These are the 15 rifles of World War II, ranked from the worst clunker ever shoved into a soldier's hands all the way up to the one gun that quietly ended an entire era of warfare. We start at the bottom. Gower 41. Germany set out to build a self-loading rifle and somehow built something worse than the bolt action it was supposed to replace. This was 1941, and the Vermacht had just met the Soviet SVT40 on the Eastern Front, a rifle that fired as fast as a soldier could pull the trigger. The Germans wanted an answer, fast, but the army handed the engineers two insane rules. Don't drill a gas port in the barrel, and don't put any moving parts on top of the weapon. So, they rigged up a bizarre muzzle cone that trapped gas at the very end of the barrel and shoved a piston backward. It worked on a bench in the mud and frost of Russia. It fouled, jammed, and weighed close to 11 lbs, heavier than the bolt gun it was meant to beat. Only about 145,000 were built before everyone admitted it was a dud. The Germans, of all people, had failed at engineering, and that failure would teach them exactly what to fix. Caro model 1891. Italy went to war with a rifle that had been showing its age since before the First World War even ended. The Carano fired a 6.5 mm round so mild that troops complained it could pass clean through an enemy without putting him down. Its end block clip had to be loaded a specific way or the whole thing choked and its sights were famously optimistic. It served across North Africa and the Eastern front strapped to men who deserve better hardware. Here's the dark irony that made it infamous, though. This obscure, unloved Italian rifle became one of the most recognized guns on the planet for a single reason. A Carano was the rifle Lee Harvey Oswald used in Dallas in 1963. A weapon nobody feared in war ended up in every history book anyway. Type 99 Arasaka. Japan's standard rifle started as a genuinely solid weapon and slowly fell apart as the Empire did. Introduced in 1939 in a harderhitting 7.7 mm, the early Type 999 was tough, accurate, and came with clever touches, a folding wire monopod, and an anti-aircraft sight on the rear leaf, as if a rifleman could swat a bomber out of the sky. Then the war turned against Japan. By 1944 and 1945, factories were churning out last ditch versions with crude fixed sights, rough stocks, and skipped machining. You can watch the craftsmanship die from one production batch to the next. On the islands of the Pacific, a well-made type 99 was respectable. A lastditch one might crack in your hands. The rifle was a mirror of a nation running out of everything. Birthier and level. France sent men into 1940 carrying rifles designed when horses were still cavalry. The label of 1886 was a genuine milestone in its day. The first rifle to use smokeless powder, but by World War II, it was a museum piece with a slow tube magazine down the barrel. Its stablemate, the Berier, loaded through a clip that held as few as three rounds while enemies carried five, eight, even 10. Both fired the ancient rimmed 8mm level cartridge, a case shaped so awkwardly it made feeding a nightmare. These rifles fought in the trenches of one world war and were still in French hands for the next. Brave soldiers, obsolete tools, and France had actually built something far better. They just built it too late. That rifle is next. And if you're enjoying this climb up the rankings, take a second to hit like and subscribe. It genuinely helps the channel. And we've still got 10 rifles to go. Each one better than the last. Mass 36. This is the tragedy of the list. A good rifle that barely got to fight. The MS36 was France's modern replacement. A clean, simple bolt action in a fresh 7.5 mm rimless round that fed far better than the old 8 mm. It was rugged and cheap to make. It had exactly one famous quirk, no safety catch at all. French doctrine said an empty chamber was the only safety a soldier needed. But the MS-36 rolled out in real numbers just as the German Blitz smashed through the Arden in May 1940. France fell in 6 weeks and the best rifle its army ever fielded spent most of the war in the hands of the enemy, the resistance and colonial troops. A quiet lesson that the finest weapon in the world is worthless if it shows up to the fight too late. Mosen Magagen M1 189130. Ugly, long, and stubborn as a mule, and the Soviets built it by the tens of millions. The Mosen's design dated back to 1891. Its bolt was famously stiff, and its rimmed cartridge was a headache. None of that mattered. What mattered was that a factory could stamp these out endlessly, and a barely trained conscript could keep one running in filth and cold that killed finer weapons. Across the entire Mosen family, production ran past 37 million rifles, more than almost any firearm in history. And in the ruins of Stalenrad, fitted with a simple 3.5 power PU scope, it became something legendary. The rifle of the Soviet sniper picking off officers across the frozen rubble, one shot at a time, crude beyond belief, and it helped bleed the German army white. 1903 Springfield. By World War II, this was the old master. Outclassed as a frontline rifle, but still deadly in the right hands, the 03 was an American mouser at heart. A boltaction 306 with a reputation for pinpoint accuracy that went back to the trenches of 1918. When the war started, plenty of Marines splashed ashore in the early Pacific fighting still carrying it because there simply weren't enough of the newer rifles to go around yet. Its real second life came through the scope. The M1903 A4 sniper variant, stripped of its iron sights and topped with optics, stayed in service picking off targets long after the line troops had moved on to something faster. A superb rifle that had the bad luck of being perfect, right? As the whole idea of the bolt action was about to be left behind. Carabiner 98K. The finest boltaction rifle ever mass-roduced and a symbol of exactly why Germany's infantry was about to be outgunned. The CAR 98K was mouser craftsmanship at its peak. a smooth, precise action, a hard-hitting 7.92 mm round, an accuracy that made it a superb sniper platform in the right hands. Roughly 14 million were built, and it armed the German soldier from the beaches of France to the gates of Moscow. But here's the trap the whole rifle sat in. No matter how beautiful the engineering, a man working a bolt by hand could fire maybe 15 aimed rounds a minute. While across the field, an American with a Garand was throwing far more lead his way without ever lowering the rifle from his shoulder. The CAR 98K wasn't beaten by a better bolt gun. It was beaten by the death of the bolt gun. Leanfield number four Mark1. If you had to fight a war with a bolt action, this was the one to hold. The British Leanfield had a trick nobody else matched. A smooth, short throw bolt and a magazine holding 10 rounds, double what most rifles carried. A trained British soldier could pour out fire so fast that German troops in both World Wars sometimes swore they were being hit by machine guns. They even had a name for the drill, the mad minute. 20, 30, sometimes more aimed shots downrange in 60 seconds. Chambered in the old rimmed 303, it fought everywhere the British went, from the hedros of Normandy to the jungles of Burma, where a shortened jungle carbine version hacked its way through the Pacific War. It was proof that a bolt action pushed to its absolute limit could still terrify. But the future belonged to rifles that didn't need a mad minute at all. Tokarev SVT40. This is the rifle that scared the Germans into copying it. The Soviet SVT40 was a gas operated semi-automatic. Pull the trigger and it cycled itself. No bolt to work. It fed [clears throat] from a 10 round magazine and let a Red Army soldier answer a German with a wall of fire instead of one careful shot. Around 1.6 million were made. It had a temper. It needed cleaning and a knowing hand. and cold mud and rushed conscripts didn't always give it either, which is why many Soviet troops went back to the trusty Mosin. But the Germans who faced it took notes, literally. When their own GA 41 flopped, engineers tore into captured SVTs to see how the gas system worked. The next German rifle would be built on lessons stolen straight off this weapon. M1 Carbine. Light as a toy and one of the most beloved weapons America ever issued. The M1 Carbine wasn't built to slug it out at long range, it fired a smaller 30 carbine round and weighed barely 5 lb, less than a bag of groceries. It was meant for the men who couldn't lug a full rifle, radio operators, machine gun crews, officers, and paratroopers who got a folding stock version they could strap tight for the jump. Soldiers loved it because it was handy, quick to shoulder, and easy to shoot. America loved it so much it built more than 6 million of them, making this featherweight carbine the single most produced American small arm of the entire war. It couldn't reach out and touch a target a Garand could. But up close, in a hedro or a jungle trail, few weapons were faster to bring to bear. G 43. Germany got it right the second time by swallowing its pride. After the humiliating GA 41, engineers threw out the ridiculous muzzle cone system and copied the clean, simple gas mechanism they'd found inside captured Soviet SVT40s. The result was the G 43, a real semi-automatic rifle at last, reliable enough to matter and simpler to build than its predecessor. But its true value showed up through glass. Fitted almost as standard with a scope mount and the ZF4 optic, the G43 became one of the best issued sniper rifles of the war, letting a German marksman fire, stay on target, and fire again without ever breaking his sight picture to work a bolt. It arrived too late and in too few numbers a few hundred,000 to change the outcome. But it was the shape of things to come and one German rifle was already reaching even further into the future. FG42, a rifle so advanced that Allied engineers dissected it after the war and lifted its ideas straight into their own designs. The FG42 was born from a disaster. The airborne invasion of Cree in 1941 where German paratroopers jumped carrying only pistols and grenades and had to sprint under fire to reach canisters holding their rifles. Never again, the planner said. So they demanded the impossible. a full power 7.92 mm rifle light enough to jump with that could fire single shots for accuracy and rip on full automatic like a light machine gun. What came out was a slender futuristic weapon with a sidemounted magazine and a muzzle that spat fire. It armed the elite faller Jagger in daring raids that stunned the allies. It was brilliant, expensive, and rare. Only around 7,000 ever made. Too costly to win a war, but its guts lived on in postwar machine guns for decades. M1 Garand, the rifle that gave the American infantrymen a superpower his enemies simply didn't have, while German and Japanese soldiers worked a bolt between every shot. The GI carrying an M1 Garand pulled the trigger eight times as fast as his thumb could move, fed by an endlock clip that ejected with a bright metallic ping when the last round was gone. It was the first semi-automatic rifle issued as standard to an entire army on Earth. And it changed what a single foot soldier could do in a firefight. More than 5 million were made and they went everywhere America fought. Omaha Beach, the frozen forests of the Arden, the black volcanic sand of Euoima. General George Patton called it the greatest battle implement ever devised. And for once, the general wasn't exaggerating. When a squad of Americans opened up, the sheer weight of fire could pin down a force twice their size. It wasn't the most accurate rifle of the war, or the most refined. It was something more important. It was the rifle that proved the future of infantry combat was self-loading. And it dragged the rest of the world's armies, kicking and yanking their bolts into a new age. And yet, even the mighty Garand was about to be made obsolete by a German weapon nobody quite understood they'd invented. Sternware 44. This is the one. Not the best rifle of World War II, the most important gun of the entire century. The Germans built it almost by accident, chasing a strange idea. What if you didn't need a giant long range cartridge at all? Most infantry firefights, they noticed, happened at a few hundred yards, not a mile. So, they shrank the round down to a 7.92 mm KURS, short cartridge, powerful enough to kill at real combat range, but tame enough to fire on full automatic without the rifle climbing off target. Then they built a weapon around it that could do everything. single aimed shots like a rifle or a controllable burst like a submachine gun fed from a 30 round magazine. Hitler reportedly hated the project at first and it had to be developed in secret disguised under code names. Around 425,000 were built far too late to save Germany. But that hardly matters now because when the war ended and engineers [clears throat] around the world pulled the STG44 apart, they all saw the same thing. The blueprint for the future. Its concept ran straight into the Soviet AK-47, into the American M16, into nearly every military rifle a soldier carries anywhere on the planet today. Every other gun on this list fought World War II. This one quietly won every war that came after it. So that's the climb. From a jammed, overweight failure the Germans themselves gave up on all the way to the weapon that made every rifle above it a relic. It's a strange thing looking back. The war was decided by bolt guns older than the men firing them. Yet, its lasting legacy was a single rifle that pointed the way out of that whole era. The past and the future, fighting side by side in the same mud. fullTextVi: Đến năm 1945, hầu hết binh lính trên Trái đất vẫn chiến đấu với thiết kế súng trường cũ hơn hơn ông nội của họ. Một cái chốt bạn phải kéo bằng tay sau mỗi lần bắn. Nhưng bị chôn vùi trong cuộc chiến đó lại là một loại vũ khí vượt xa mọi người khác mà hôm nay người lính vẫn cõng cháu mình ra trận. Đây là 15 khẩu súng trường trong Thế chiến II, được xếp hạng từ loại súng trường tệ nhất từng bị đẩy vào tay người lính cho đến tận một khẩu súng đã lặng lẽ kết thúc cả một kỷ nguyên chiến tranh. Chúng tôi bắt đầu ở phía dưới. Gower 41. Đức bắt đầu chế tạo súng trường tự nạp đạn và bằng cách nào đó đã chế tạo được thứ còn tệ hơn hành động bu lông mà nó được cho là sẽ thay thế. Đó là năm 1941, và Vermacht vừa gặp SVT40 của Liên Xô trên Mặt trận phía Đông, một khẩu súng trường bắn nhanh như một người lính có thể kéo cò súng. Người Đức muốn có câu trả lời nhanh chóng, nhưng quân đội đã giao cho các kỹ sư hai kẻ điên rồ quy tắc. Không khoan cổng khí trong thùng và không đặt bất kỳ bộ phận chuyển động nào phía trên vũ khí. Vì vậy, họ đã chế tạo một chiếc mõm hình nón kỳ quái có chức năng giữ khí ở ngay cuối thùng và đẩy pít-tông về phía sau. Nó làm việc trên một chiếc ghế dài trong bùn và băng giá ở Nga. Nó bám bẩn, kẹt giấy và nặng gần 11 lbs, nặng hơn cả súng bắn tia nó nhằm mục đích đánh bại. Chỉ có khoảng 145.000 chiếc được chế tạo trước khi mọi người thừa nhận nó là một chiếc xe ngu ngốc. Người Đức, trong số tất cả mọi người, đã thất bại trong lĩnh vực kỹ thuật, và thất bại đó sẽ dạy cho họ chính xác những gì cần sửa chữa. Mẫu caro 1891. Ý gây chiến với khẩu súng trường đã có tuổi từ lâu thậm chí trước khi Thế chiến thứ nhất kết thúc. Carano bắn quả 6. Tròn 5 mm nhẹ đến mức quân đội phàn nàn rằng nó có thể xuyên qua kẻ thù mà không hạ gục hắn. Clip khối cuối của nó phải được tải theo một cách cụ thể hoặc toàn bộ mọi thứ bị bóp nghẹt và tầm nhìn của nó nổi tiếng là lạc quan. Nó phục vụ trên khắp Bắc Phi và mặt trận phía Đông dành cho những người đàn ông xứng đáng phần cứng tốt hơn. Tuy nhiên, đây chính là điều trớ trêu đen tối đã khiến nó trở nên khét tiếng. Khẩu súng trường Ý ít người biết đến này đã trở thành một trong những loại súng được biết đến nhiều nhất trên hành tinh vì một lý do duy nhất. Carano là khẩu súng trường Lee Harvey Oswald sử dụng ở Dallas năm 1963. Dù sao đi nữa, một loại vũ khí mà không ai sợ hãi trong chiến tranh lại xuất hiện trong mọi cuốn sách lịch sử. Kiểu 99 Arasaka. Súng trường tiêu chuẩn của Nhật Bản bắt đầu như một loại vũ khí thực sự vững chắc và dần dần tan rã khi Đế chế đã làm. Sau đó chiến tranh quay lưng lại với Nhật Bản. Đến năm 1944 và 1945, các nhà máy đã sản xuất ra những phiên bản cuối cùng với dầu thô cố định điểm tham quan, cổ phiếu thô và bỏ qua gia công. Những khẩu súng trường này đã chiến đấu trong chiến hào của một cuộc chiến tranh thế giới và vẫn còn ở Tay Pháp cho người tiếp theo. Mỗi cái tốt hơn cái cuối cùng. Thánh lễ 36. Đây chính là bi kịch của danh sách. Một khẩu súng trường tốt mà hầu như không phải chiến đấu. MS36 là sự thay thế hiện đại của Pháp. Đến Thế chiến II, đây là bậc thầy cũ. Vượt trội hơn so với súng trường tiền tuyến, nhưng vẫn gây chết người khi sử dụng tay phải, khẩu 03 thực chất là một tay săn chuột người Mỹ. Một chốt khóa 306 nổi tiếng về độ chính xác tuyệt đối đã quay trở lại chiến hào năm 1918. Khi chiến tranh bắt đầu, rất nhiều lính thủy đánh bộ đã tràn vào bờ trong cuộc giao tranh đầu tiên ở Thái Bình Dương vẫn mang nó vì đơn giản là không có đủ súng trường mới hơn để sử dụng xung quanh chưa. Cuộc sống thứ hai thực sự của nó đến từ phạm vi. Biến thể bắn tỉa M1903 A4, loại bỏ ống ngắm bằng sắt và đứng đầu với hệ thống quang học, ở lại phục vụ để tiêu diệt mục tiêu rất lâu sau khi quân tuyến đã di chuyển đến một cái gì đó nhanh hơn.
